agent: Claude Code (CLAUDE.md, this repository) — WP-03a verification: item (vi), loop.counts (PASSES/FAILURES)
summary_for_principal:
This closes another sub-part of the same checklist item as the last three PRs (declared settings the system accepts but doesn't fully act on).

A loop in a process can be set to give up after too many repeats. The format lets an author say those repeats should only count when a check actually failed, not every time the loop runs — but that setting was silently ignored everywhere; every repeat counted, no matter what was declared.

Fixed where it's genuinely well-defined: when a decision point (not a plain routing choice) is what triggers the loop, 'a check failed' has one clear meaning — a decision that says no. That case now works correctly. For an ordinary routing choice (an if/then branch on some value), there's no reliable way for the system to know which branch represents 'a check failed' versus an unrelated path, so declaring that setting there is now refused with a clear message rather than silently doing the wrong thing or guessing.

Full test suite: 371 passed, 4 new.

Numbered actions:
1. Nothing needs deciding right now.
2. Two larger, riskier sub-parts of this item remain, plus three unrelated items.

interpretation.ask_as_given: Verify item (vi)'s 'inert accepted fields' half: a background research pass found loop.counts (PASSES/FAILURES) accepted, parsed, and never read anywhere — every loop take counts toward its budget regardless of verdict.
interpretation.read_as: Determine whether 'because a check failed' has an engine-derivable meaning at all for the two places a loop budget is actually enforced (ROUTE, GATE), implement it where it does, and refuse rather than guess where it doesn't — rather than either implementing a fragile heuristic for both, or leaving the whole field undocumented as equally inert everywhere.

filled_in.gap: The spec's 'because a check failed' is not defined in terms of any specific engine-visible signal — it's a plain-language description that happens to map cleanly onto GATE's own ADR-028 verdict vocabulary but not onto ROUTE's arbitrary state expressions.
filled_in.assumed: For GATE: a DENY verdict IS 'a check failed' — DECIDED only ever carries PERMIT or DENY, and DENY is ADR-028's own negative outcome, so no invention is needed. For ROUTE: nothing in a `when` branch's own shape tells the engine whether it represents a failure, so implementing FAILURES there would require guessing at author intent from branch naming or condition shape — refused instead, following the same 'refuse rather than guess' precedent D26 (kind: INPUT) and D27 (note_into's reducer restriction) already established this session.
filled_in.grounded_in: CLAUDE.md's 'fail closed' and 'survive the bad-but-conformant attack' — a heuristic that infers 'failure' from a when-branch's condition text would itself be the kind of invented, unstated rule these principles refuse to let code guess at.
filled_in.reversal_cost: Low for both halves — the GATE implementation is a local conditional with no schema change; the ROUTE refusals are early-return checks a future pass (with a principal-approved schema mechanism for marking a failure branch) could remove without touching anything else.

filled_in.gap: Whether a take that doesn't count under FAILURES semantics should still be subject to the budget check at all, or skip it entirely, isn't stated by the spec's own two-sentence description.
filled_in.assumed: Skip the budget check entirely for a non-counting take — the budget exists to bound repeated FAILURES specifically ('only when taken because a check failed' describes what's being limited), so a passing take should never be blocked by a failure count it isn't part of.
filled_in.grounded_in: The plain reading of 'only when taken because a check failed' as describing the budget's own scope of concern, not merely which takes get tallied while all takes remain subject to the same ceiling.
filled_in.reversal_cost: Low — a one-line conditional guarding the existing check_loop_budget call.

decisions.headline: D33 — loop.counts: FAILURES is implemented for a GATE's own looping verdict route (a take counts only when the resolving verdict is DENY) and refused, at both validation (V8) and engine runtime, for a ROUTE loop.
decisions.problem: loop.counts was accepted, parsed, and carried by every LoopSpec, but nothing in engine/routes.py or engine/run.py ever read it — every loop take counted toward its budget regardless of verdict, exactly PASSES semantics, whatever counts actually said.
options_rejected: Infer 'failure' from a ROUTE when-branch's own naming convention (e.g. a condition referencing a .verdict/.passed-shaped path): rejected — fragile, guesses at author intent from string shape, breaks the moment a real condition doesn't match the guessed pattern.

Add a new schema field marking a ROUTE when option as the failure branch: rejected for this pass — new schema surface decided unilaterally, without the worked-example precedent this format's other decisions have had; left as a proposed future spec change instead.
decisions.cost_to_change: Low for both halves — see interpretation.filled_in above.

lessons.maxim: Before implementing 'the same fix' across multiple node kinds that share a schema field, check whether the field's own semantics are actually symmetric across those kinds — GATE and ROUTE both accept loop.counts, but only one of them has an engine-visible signal the field's own definition can attach to.
lessons.incident: A naive implementation might have tried one heuristic (e.g. inferring failure from a when-branch's condition text) to make FAILURES work identically for both ROUTE and GATE loops; checking each kind's own actual resolution mechanism first (GATE's fixed PERMIT/DENY vocabulary vs ROUTE's arbitrary state expressions) revealed they needed two different answers — implement for one, refuse for the other — rather than one uniform (and for ROUTE, necessarily guessed) mechanism.
lessons.destination: D33's own MADR entry documents both halves and why they differ.
lessons.proposed_check: When a schema field is declared generically across multiple node kinds, verify each kind's own resolution mechanism actually supports the field's stated semantics before assuming one implementation covers all of them.
